{{short description|French historian of mathematics and sinologist (born 1957)}}
{{Use dmy dates|cs1-dates=ly|date=December 2023}}
[[File:Karine Chemla (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright=0.85|Chemla at [[Mathematical Research Institute of Oberwolfach]] in 2009]]

'''Karine Chemla''' (born 8 February 1957) is a French [[history of mathematics|historian of mathematics]] and [[Sinology|sinologist]] who works as a director of research at the [[Centre national de la recherche scientifique]] (CNRS).<ref name=cnrs /> She is also a senior fellow at the [[New York University]] [[Institute for the Study of the Ancient World]].<ref>{{citation|url=http://isaw.nyu.edu/people/senior-fellows/karine-chemla-1|title=Karine Chemla|work=Senior Fellows|date=23 October 2012|publisher=NYU ISAW|accessdate=2015-10-15}}.</ref> She was elected a Member of the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 2019.

== Education ==
Chemla studied at [[Paris Diderot University]] and the [[École normale supérieure de jeunes filles]], earning an [[agrégation]] in mathematics in 1978 and a [[Master of Advanced Studies|diploma of advanced studies]] in 1979.<ref name="leo-cv" /> At this time, her work was in pure mathematics. However, in 1980, influenced by the work of [[Ilya Prigogine]], she won a Singer–Polignac scholarship to travel to China and study the history of Chinese mathematics.<ref name="laudatio">{{citation|title=Laudatio Karine Chemla|first=Liesbeth|last=De Mol|pages=9–12|journal=Sartoniana|volume=27|year=2014|url=http://www.sartonchair.ugent.be/file/288}}.</ref> Returning to France, she earned her Ph.D. in the history of mathematics from [[Paris 13 University]] in 1982, and began working for CNRS at that time.<ref name="leo-cv">{{citation|url=http://www.leopoldina.org/fileadmin/redaktion/Mitglieder/CV_Chemla_Karine_EN.pdf|title=Curriculum vitae: Karine Chemla|publisher=Leopoldina|accessdate=2015-10-15}}.</ref>

== Contributions ==
Chemla's research interests include [[Chinese mathematics]], 19th century French [[geometry]], and the theory of the history of mathematics.<ref name=cnrs>{{citation|url=http://www.sphere.univ-paris-diderot.fr/spip.php?article78&lang=en|title=CHEMLA Karine|publisher=Lab. SPHERE (Sciences, Philosophy, History), CNRS|accessdate=2015-10-15}}.</ref>

With Guo Shuchun, Chemla published in 2004 a critical edition and translation into French of ''[[The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art]]''.<ref name="laudatio" /><ref>{{citation

 | volume = 37
 | year = 2010| doi-access =

 | jstor = 4529052
 | pages = 511–513

 | year = 2006}}.</ref><ref>{{citation

== Recognition ==
Chemla was an [[list of International Congresses of Mathematicians Plenary and Invited Speakers|invited speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1998.<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.mathunion.org/icm-plenary-and-invited-speakers?combine=Chemla|title=ICM Plenary and Invited Speakers since 1897|publisher=[[International Mathematical Union]]|accessdate=2015-10-01}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|last=Chemla|first=Karine|chapter=History of Mathematics: A Factor in World History and a Source for New Questions|title=Doc. Math. (Bielefeld) Extra Vol. ICM Berlin, 1998, vol. III|year=1998|pages=789–798|chapter-url=https://www.elibm.org/ft/10011633000}}</ref>
She became a member of the [[Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]] in 2004,<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.leopoldina.org/en/members/list-of-members/member/1079/|title=Prof. Dr. Karine Chemla|work=List of Members|publisher=Leopoldina|accessdate=2015-10-15}}.</ref> of the [[International Academy of the History of Science]] in 2005,<ref name="leo-cv" /> and of the [[Academia Europaea]] in 2013.<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.ae-info.org/ae/User/Chemla_Karine|title=Member profile: Karine Chemla|publisher=Academia Europaea|accessdate=2015-10-15}}.</ref> In 2013–2014 she was the holder of the Sarton Chair of History of Science at [[Ghent University]].<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.sartonchair.ugent.be/en/pastchairholders|title=Sarton Chair of History of Science: Past chair holders|publisher=Ghent University|accessdate=2015-10-15}}.</ref> She served as president of the European Society for the History of Science 2014–2016.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scientific Board |url=https://www.eshs.org/scientific-board/ |access-date=November 29, 2024 |website=European Society for the History of Science}}</ref> She is the 2020 winner of the Otto Neugebauer Prize<ref>{{citation|url=https://euro-math-soc.eu/news/20/05/8/prize-winners-announced|title=Prize Winners Announced|publisher=European Mathematical Society|date=8 May 2020|access-date=2020-05-08 |archive-date=2020-12-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201230123245/https://euro-math-soc.eu/news/20/05/8/prize-winners-announced|url-status=dead}}</ref> and the 2021 winner of the [[LMS-BSHM Hirst Prize]].
